entries.headline: Arup: a fake video call with fake colleagues
entries.what: A finance worker at engineering firm Arup joined a video call with fake versions of his UK finance chief and colleagues, then made 15 transfers worth HK$200 million (about US$25.6M).
entries.how: Police said fraudsters likely used public video and audio plus AI-made voices. He doubted a suspicious email at first, then trusted the call.
entries.fixed: It came to light when he checked with head office. Arup said its systems were not affected. No arrests or recovery were reported; still under investigation at the last report found.
entries.protect: Treat any video call asking for urgent, secret payments as suspect, and confirm through a separate channel.

entries.headline: Change Healthcare: US health payments frozen
entries.what: Ransomware (the ALPHV/BlackCat group) disrupted insurance claims and payments across the US. A reported 192.7 million people were affected, per a 2025 filing.
entries.how: Stolen login details worked on a remote-access portal with no second login step, according to the parent company's CEO.
entries.fixed: A ransom of about $22M was reportedly paid, and the gang then reportedly vanished. Free credit monitoring was offered. Lawsuits are combined in one court; no settlement as of 30 September 2026.
entries.protect: Use a different password for each account, with two-step login switched on.

entries.headline: MOVEit: one flaw, thousands of organisations
entries.what: The Clop group stole data from servers running MOVEit, a file-transfer product. A researcher counted about 2,095 organisations and around 62 million people by September 2023 (an estimate).
entries.how: A previously unknown flaw let attackers send commands to the product's database. The maker, Progress Software, released a fix on 31 May 2023.
entries.fixed: Lawsuits are combined in one US case. A $2.5M settlement with Ernst & Young and Bank of America got final approval in October 2026. Claims against Progress continue. No arrests found.
entries.protect: If you're told your data was involved, freeze your credit and watch for fake messages.

entries.headline: AIIMS Delhi: a hospital forced onto paper
entries.what: Ransomware took AIIMS Delhi's servers offline. Outpatient, inpatient and lab services ran on paper for over a week.
entries.how: The IT minister told Parliament 5 servers and about 1.3 TB of data were encrypted. Early analysis pointed to poor separation between parts of the network.
entries.fixed: AIIMS said hospital data was restored on 29 November 2022. No arrests reported. Unnamed officials said it came from China; that is not confirmed. A reported Rs 200 crore demand was not confirmed to police.
entries.protect: Hospitals and offices should keep offline backups and keep parts of their network separate.

entries.headline: Optus: 9.5 million Australians' details leaked
entries.what: About 9.5 million Australians' names, birth dates, phone numbers and emails leaked. About 2.4 million also had ID numbers exposed.
entries.how: An internet-facing system lacked a proper login check, so attackers could pull other customers' records by changing numbers in the web address.
entries.fixed: In August 2025 the privacy regulator took Optus to court. As of 4 October 2026 there was no decision, and the communications regulator's case has no public outcome. No arrests found.
entries.protect: Give companies only the data they need, and be wary of messages after any breach.

entries.headline: Air India: 4.5 million passengers' data exposed
entries.what: About 4.5 million passengers' details from 2011 to 2021 were exposed: names, birth dates, passport and ticket details, some card data and frequent-flyer data. No card security codes or passwords.
entries.how: The breach was at SITA, the company that runs Air India's passenger system. SITA confirmed it on 24 February 2021.
entries.fixed: SITA secured its servers. Air India investigated with outside experts, told card companies and reset frequent-flyer passwords. No arrests or penalties are publicly reported.
entries.protect: Use a different password for each travel account, and check your card statements after a breach notice.

entries.headline: Colonial Pipeline: fuel supply stopped for days
entries.what: Ransomware (the DarkSide group) hit the company's business network. The pipeline shut for nearly a week and over 9,500 petrol stations ran dry.
entries.how: Attackers used an old, unused remote-access account that had no second login step.
entries.fixed: The company paid about $4.4M in bitcoin. In June 2021 the US Justice Department recovered about $2.3M of it. No arrests were found in the sources opened.
entries.protect: Turn on two-step login and delete accounts you no longer use.

entries.headline: Ireland's health service locked by ransomware
entries.what: Ransomware (the Conti group) locked about 80 percent of the health service's IT. Hospitals cancelled some services and data was stolen.
entries.how: A staff member opened a malicious spreadsheet attachment, and attackers stayed inside about eight weeks. A review found an outdated, poorly separated network.
entries.fixed: Ireland did not pay. A decryption key was released on 20 May and systems recovered by September 2021, at a cost of about €51M in 2021.
entries.protect: Don't open unexpected attachments, even from someone you know, and keep systems updated.

entries.headline: Log4Shell: a flaw hidden inside countless apps
entries.what: A top-severity flaw (10 out of 10) in Log4j, a free tool used inside huge numbers of apps and servers, led to mass scanning and attacks.
entries.how: A feature of the tool could be tricked into loading outside instructions from ordinary text. It had existed since 2013.
entries.fixed: The maker released fixes between 10 and 28 December 2021. A US government review in July 2022 called it an "endemic vulnerability" likely to linger for years.
entries.protect: Keep apps and devices updated, and ask a company whether it uses Log4j after a warning.

entries.headline: SolarWinds: booby-trapped software updates
entries.what: Booby-trapped updates from SolarWinds reached up to about 18,000 customers. Around 100 were broken into, including US government departments, Microsoft and FireEye.
entries.how: Attackers got into the company's software-building system and slipped a hidden backdoor into signed updates.
entries.fixed: In April 2021 the US and UK attributed it to Russia's foreign intelligence service and the US imposed sanctions. The US regulator's case against SolarWinds was dropped in 2025. No arrests.
entries.protect: Install updates from trusted makers promptly, and keep watching for odd behaviour afterwards.

entries.headline: A cloned voice moved $35 million
entries.what: A UAE bank manager got a call from a voice like a company director he knew, asking for $35 million for an acquisition. Emails from a "lawyer" backed it up, and he approved it.
entries.how: Forbes reported the voice was cloned with "deep voice" technology. The bank was not named.
entries.fixed: Money went to several countries; about $415,000 reached two US accounts. Court filings cite at least 17 people. Recovery and outcome not publicly reported.
entries.protect: Never approve a large transfer on a phone call and an email alone; always get a second, separate check.
sources: AI Business (summary of the Forbes report)

entries.headline: Kudankulam nuclear plant: malware on the office network
entries.what: Malware called Dtrack was found on a computer on the plant's office network. Operator NPCIL said the systems that run the reactors were separate and unaffected.
entries.how: Security firm Dragos found plant-specific names in the malware, suggesting a targeted attack. How it got in is not publicly reported.
entries.fixed: NPCIL confirmed it on 30 October 2019 and said it was contained. The plant kept operating. No arrests reported and no official blame named.
entries.protect: Keep office and control networks strictly apart, and never reuse passwords between them.

entries.headline: The first reported AI voice-clone payment scam
entries.what: The head of a UK energy firm took a call from someone he believed was his German boss and sent €220,000 (about $243,000) to a Hungarian supplier.
entries.how: Analysts quoted in the report believe AI software copied the boss's voice and accent. The caller demanded payment "within an hour".
entries.fixed: The money moved on to other countries. The victim grew suspicious at a second call and paid no more. Recovery and arrests not publicly reported.
entries.protect: For any urgent payment request, call the person back on a number you already have.
sources: Dark Reading (summary of the Wall Street Journal report)

entries.headline: Cosmos Bank, Pune: Rs 94 crore taken in three days
entries.what: About Rs 94.42 crore (about $13.5M) was taken, mostly through card withdrawals abroad, plus a transfer to a Hong Kong account.
entries.how: Malware on the bank's card-payment system let attackers approve withdrawals with fake messages. A security firm suggested a phishing email as the likely way in.
entries.fixed: Pune cyber police arrested 7 people by 19 September 2018. A security firm linked it to the North Korea-connected Lazarus group; Indian authorities have not confirmed that. Court outcome not publicly reported.
entries.protect: Tell your bank at once about any card debit you don't recognise.

entries.headline: Equifax: 147 million people's data taken
entries.what: About 147 million people's data was taken, including 145.5 million Social Security numbers.
entries.how: An Apache Struts flaw on a dispute portal went unpatched for four months. Plain-text credentials and weak network separation let attackers go further.
entries.fixed: In July 2019 Equifax agreed to pay at least $575M and up to $700M to US regulators and states. In February 2020 the US charged four members of China's PLA 54th Research Institute; they are not in custody.
entries.protect: Freeze your credit and use a unique password for every site.

entries.headline: NotPetya: $10 billion in damage from a fake ransomware
entries.what: Wiper malware disguised as ransomware hit mainly Ukraine, plus Maersk, Merck and FedEx/TNT. Estimated global losses passed $10B.
entries.how: It spread through a poisoned update to Ukrainian tax software M.E.Doc, then moved across networks with the same flaw WannaCry used.
entries.fixed: Ukraine, the US and the UK attributed it to Russia, which denies it. In 2020 the US charged six Russian officers, four over NotPetya. They remain at large.
entries.protect: Patch promptly and keep offline backups.

entries.headline: WannaCry: the NHS cancels 19,000 appointments
entries.what: Ransomware demanding about $300 in bitcoin hit organisations worldwide. The UK's NHS lost about £92M and cancelled more than 19,000 appointments and operations.
entries.how: It spread through a Windows file-sharing flaw (EternalBlue) leaked in April 2017. Microsoft had patched it on 14 March 2017.
entries.fixed: Researcher Marcus Hutchins registered a hidden "kill switch" domain that slowed the spread. The US government attributed it to North Korea. No attackers arrested.
entries.protect: Install Windows updates promptly and retire unsupported systems.

entries.headline: Mirai: smart gadgets used to knock out the internet
entries.what: An attack on DNS provider Dyn disrupted much of the US East Coast internet.
entries.how: The Mirai botnet scanned for cameras, routers and recorders still using default passwords and took them over.
entries.fixed: Three authors pleaded guilty in December 2017. Each got five years' probation, 2,500 hours of community service and $127,000 restitution after cooperating.
entries.protect: Change default passwords and update the firmware on smart devices.

entries.headline: Bangladesh Bank: $81 million stolen through SWIFT
entries.what: About $81M was stolen from the bank's account at the New York Fed. A further $20M transfer was stopped after a spelling error was noticed.
entries.how: Spear-phishing gave attackers access to SWIFT-connected computers, and they sent fraudulent payment instructions.
entries.fixed: The Philippine central bank fined RCBC about $21M. About $15M was recovered by early 2018. The US charged North Korean national Park Jin Hyok and attributes the attack to a North Korea-backed group.
entries.protect: Treat unexpected attachments and links, even "job applications", as suspect.

entries.headline: Target: 40 million cards exposed at Christmas
entries.what: Up to 40 million card accounts were exposed during the holiday season.
entries.how: Attackers used credentials stolen from a third-party vendor to reach Target's network, per the New York Attorney General.
entries.fixed: In May 2017 Target paid $18.5M to 47 states and DC and agreed to add a security executive and an outside security assessment. Target put its total cost at $202M.
entries.protect: Watch card statements and turn on card alerts.

entries.headline: Stuxnet: the worm that damaged machines
entries.what: A worm reprogrammed Siemens controllers at Iran's Natanz plant. A think-tank report says about 1,000 centrifuges were replaced between late 2009 and early 2010.
entries.how: It reportedly entered via a USB drive and used four Microsoft zero-day flaws, while showing operators normal readings.
entries.fixed: No state has claimed it; the US and Israel are widely speculated, with no concrete evidence. It is seen as the first cyber-attack with destructive physical effects.
entries.protect: Keep industrial and office networks separate and block unknown USB drives.
